To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a class B scavengereceptor mediates cellular carotenoid uptake in Drosophilia.

a Drosophila gene encoding a class B scavenging receptor mediates the uptake of dietary carotenoids and that a loss of this gene results in the blindness of Drosophila larvae due to the lack of visual chromophore formation.
a scavenger receptor is essential for carotenoid uptake and vitamin A formation in flies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms underlying the formation of the vitamin A precursor from carotenoids.

the elucidation of the biochemical and molecular mechanisms underlying the formation of the vitamin A chromophore in invertebrates and the elucidation of how the uptake of carotenoid pigments is regulated in the animal cell.
a new function of scavenger receptors in carotenoid metabolism and with a new role of carotenoids for the health of the animal.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Drosophila ninaD gene product is a class B scavenging receptor for dietary carotenoids and that it is required for the formation of 11-cis-retinol, the visual chromophores, and for the formation of retinol from carotenoids.
the ninaD gene product is a class B scavenging receptor that mediates the cellular internalization and uptake of carotenoid molecules.

the ninaD gene product is a scavenger receptor that mediates the cellular transport of carotenoids, and that the ninaE gene product, a member of the same gene family, mediates the cellular import of retinoids.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ninaD encodes a carotenoid scavenger receptor that is essential for the uptake of carotenoid precursors of vitamin A and that this uptake is required for the formation of visual chromophore.

a scavenger receptor is essential for the uptake of carotenoid precursors of the vitamin A molecule into cells, and that the resulting lack of the vitamin A-former enzyme leads to a carotenoid- and vitamin A-free phenotype in the Drosophila eye.

the ninaD gene is essential to the formation of the chromophore for the visual pigments of the Drosophila compound eyes, and that this gene is also required for the uptake of dietary carotenoids into Drosophila cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
scavenger receptor class B type 2 is required for the uptake of carotenoid into the eye of the fruit fly.
scavenger receptors play an important role in carotenoid metabolism in Drosophilla and that this may be true in humans.
the scavenger receptor encoded by the ninaD gene is essential for the formation the visual chromophores in the Drosophila eye.
